extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article summarizing the events, investigation, controversy, and aftermath of a high-profile criminal allegation and prosecutorial misconduct. Aimed at providing a comprehensive, sourced narrative of the Duke lacrosse case and related institutional/media issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo identification: include non-suspect fillers
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. Department of Justice guidelines suggest including at least five non-suspect filler photos for each suspect included; the Durham Police Department's own General Order 4077 recommended including fillers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present photo arrays composed only of suspected individuals. Include multiple filler photos so the witness is not forced to pick from only suspects; avoid procedures that cue a positive identification (anti-pattern: suspect-only arrays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo identification: present arrays, not isolated projections
rubrics_metrics.description: In this case, 'the photos were shown to Mangum as a PowerPoint presentation, with each photo projected individually to her, rather than the pictures being arrayed together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display photos as simultaneous arrays rather than projecting one photo at a time; individual projection can be suggestive and lead to unreliable identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo identification: avoid leading / suggestive procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense attorneys described the process as essentially a 'multiple-choice test in which there were no wrong answers'; James Earl Coleman Jr. stated an officer was, in effect, telling the witness 'Pick three.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators must avoid wording or procedures that suggest the expected answer, avoid implying all shown people are suspects, and avoid repeated identifications that can increase (but not improve) witness confidence. (Expert note: 'memory does not improve with time.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to internal police policies and neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Durham Police Department was criticized for 'violating their own policies by allowing Nifong to act as the de facto head of the investigation' and for distributing a poster that appeared to presume the suspects' guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police must follow departmental rules (e.g., who coordinates investigations), avoid actions that presume guilt, and preserve investigative neutrality in communications and public materials. Anti-patterns: letting a prosecutor dominate investigative control inappropriately; public materials implying guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using coercive or intimidatory tactics on witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported arrests and pressure (e.g., arresting a taxi driver who refused to alter testimony) were criticized as attempts to influence witness testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should not leverage arrests, pending charges, or immigration status to coerce witnesses into changing statements. Such tactics undermine reliability and can constitute misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial conduct: avoid prejudicial public statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The North Carolina bar filed ethics charges against Nifong for 'making public statements that were prejudicial to the administration of justice and heightened public condemnation of the accused.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors should refrain from public commentary that could prejudice proceedings or sway public opinion against defendants. Anti-patterns: frequent media interviews asserting guilt, publicizing untested theories or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial honesty and disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nifong was accused of 'dishonesty, fraud, deceit and misrepresentation' and of withholding DNA evidence; later disbarred for trial conduct and found guilty of criminal contempt for lying about sharing DNA tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors must honestly represent facts and disclose exculpatory or materially relevant evidence to the defense (Brady-type obligations). Withholding or misrepresenting forensic findings is ethical and legal misconduct with severe consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forensic laboratory reporting: full disclosure of findings
rubrics_metrics.description: DNA Security Inc. produced an incomplete report and 'deliberately withheld information' from the lab's report; the defense argued the report omitted information showing none of the team matched certain genetic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forensic labs must report complete findings and not omit exculpatory data. Lab directors and technicians should follow lab policies and legal obligations to disclose all relevant analytic results; withholding exclusions or details is an anti-pattern and may violate policy and law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of contamination and secondary transfer in DNA interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense contested that any DNA on fingernail samples could have come from tissue paper, cotton swabs, or other hygiene-related trash in the garbage can; SBI experts later confirmed transfer was plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting DNA results, analysts and investigators must consider alternative transfer mechanisms, environmental contamination, and whether the presence of DNA denotes direct contact or secondary transfer. Explain uncertainty and population-exclusion statistics clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exploit investigations for political advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers suggested Nifong's prosecution and public statements may have been motivated by his ongoing election campaign and desire to attract voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials should avoid allowing political considerations to influence charging decisions, public statements, or investigative priorities. Using high-profile cases for political gain undermines fairness and prosecutorial ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media discretion on revealing accuser/accused identities in sexual-assault reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Several major broadcasters did not publish the accuser's name at any point, while others revealed her photo or name after dismissal; the article lists which outlets revealed or withheld identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should weigh privacy, legal, and ethical considerations when deciding whether to publish the names or images of sexual-assault accusers or (in some cases) accused persons; practicing restraint is common among many outlets (anti-pattern: publishing identity without clear editorial justification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accurate, contemporaneous investigative notes and disclosure of inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The case drew criticism for pursuing the prosecution 'despite vast discrepancies in notes taken by Investigator Benjamin Himan and Sergeant Mark Gottlieb' and for other investigative irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should keep accurate, contemporaneous records, reconcile discrepancies promptly, and disclose inconsistent reports to defense counsel where required. Failure to do so can undermine credibility and fairness of proceedings.
